Both Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2I and Roussy-Levy syndrome arise from haploinsufficiency of the MPZ gene, which is crucial for the formation and maintenance of peripheral nerve myelin. Reduced MPZ levels disrupt the structural integrity and function of Schwann cells, leading to demyelination and axonal degeneration, manifesting as a shared phenotype of peripheral neuropathy, and contributing to specific overlapping phenotypes such as pes cavus, scoliosis, tremor, and areflexia.

#### 1. Roussy-Levy syndrome  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.786)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-9619665)

Both Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2I and Roussy-Levy syndrome arise from haploinsufficiency of the MPZ gene, which is crucial for the formation and maintenance of peripheral nerve myelin. Reduced MPZ levels disrupt the structural integrity and function of Schwann cells, leading to demyelination and axonal degeneration, manifesting as a shared phenotype of peripheral neuropathy, and contributing to specific overlapping phenotypes such as pes cavus, scoliosis, tremor, and areflexia.

**How to falsify it:** Demonstration that mutations in MPZ cause loss-of-function in one disease and gain-of-function in the other, or identification of a distinct causal gene for one of the diseases with no overlap in affected pathways. _(variant: Lack of pathogenic variants in MPZ in large population databases (e.g., gnomAD) for individuals presenting with these phenotypes would challenge the causal role of MPZ.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared mechanism in MPZ provides a unified target for therapeutic strategies aimed at promoting myelin repair or enhancing MPZ protein stability/function in both Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2I and Roussy-Levy syndrome patients.
